cells.tense: You are here at the table with the pen, and the scattered pieces are coming into one line.
cells.ask: Before the next hard conversation, write down the two things that actually matter and read them once. Let the rest wait outside.
cells.core:
You can gather what's scattered and still stay in the room with people. That's the part that's working: you hold several threads at once and you don't lose the person while you sort them. When a hard conversation opens up, you're not managing it from above — you're in it, and the pieces still come together.

That's rare, and it's yours to keep. The fairness underneath it isn't something you calculate; it shows up in how you give and take without keeping score. So the invitation here is small. Pick the next hard conversation, write down what actually matters before you walk in, and let that be enough. You don't need to hold everything to stay fair. You just need to know which two things you're carrying.

cells.tense: You will have this worked out in advance, every version of it, before anyone has said a word.
cells.ask: In the next conversation, say what you actually feel first, before the plan. Let the direction come out of that instead of the other way around.
cells.core:
You're running the conversation ahead of time. Every version of it, every turn, already mapped into a strategy — and that work is eating the thing it was meant to serve. You walk in with the whole picture and the other person can feel they can't move without breaking it.

The gathering was meant to serve the connection. Instead it stands in front of it. Less thinking isn't the answer — it's letting the thinking come after the feeling instead of before it. Say what you actually feel, once, and let the plan find its shape from there. The alignment you're reaching for won't come from getting ahead of the moment. It comes from moving with it.

cells.tense: You were standing at the door of this a long time ago, and you are still standing there.
cells.ask: Sit with one feeling for ten minutes without fixing it or explaining it. Don't bring it to anyone. Just let it be there and notice what it knows.
cells.core:
The gathering stopped. Lines that used to come together now stay apart, and you've gotten used to not being in the room while it happens — present enough to nod, not present enough to actually meet anyone. The connection you're capable of hasn't gone anywhere. It's just not being fed.

What's missing first isn't more effort with people. It's time with your own knowing, quietly. Let one feeling sit with you without taking it anywhere or doing anything about it. That's where the current returns from, not from pushing yourself into more contact than you can give. When you can sit with what you feel, the room becomes possible again. Not tonight, necessarily. But from there.

cells.tense: You are already bringing people back to each other in that room, and you talk about it as if it were just how things go.
cells.ask: Name one thing you did that brought people back to each other this week, and say out loud that you did it. Not the situation — you.
cells.core:
In conversation, you're the one who finds the line between what people said and what they meant — and you've been calling that just paying attention. It's yours, and it runs whether you claim it or not.

From the inside it looks like common sense. From across the table it's the thing that lets people land back with each other. Some of that came from people who taught you how to hold a room, and that's real. But you're the one doing it now, live, in the moment, adapting it to whoever is in front of you. That part is yours, not borrowed. Claim one piece of it this week and the rest gets easier to see.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that the person is gathering thoughts into alignment at all — the record only licenses describing what the capacity does, not asserting it is running in any given moment. A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not the one gathering anything, the situation is.' The ask survives being wrong because it is a single visible act — writing something down and reading it once — not a claim about their inner life. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you're the one who holds it together for everyone,' which flatters the reader and puts a role on the person instead of an offer.
